title: Global Value Investing | Thomas Russo | Talks at Google
description:
“I consider myself to be a farmer—not a hunter. And I think most people on Wall Street are hunters. They like to fell big beasts and I’m very comfortable planting a few rows and just tending to them carefully.” - Thomas Russo

About the Talk
Mr. Russo looks forward to describing how that in his pursuit of long-term tax-deferred investment returns that he has favored investments in businesses whose global brands are well-position companies for reinvestment of mature market free cash flow into developing and emerging markets. Mr. Russo’s businesses accordingly possess the “capacity to reinvest” and managements who have the “capacity to suffer” when investments properly intended for longest term increase in intrinsic value on a per share basis burden as they often do, reported earnings in the near term. 

This tradeoff between near-term pain and long-term gain is at the heart of his investments when properly executed, the benefit for taxable investors is the ability to build portfolio companies whose return are long term and tax deferred. 

About the Speaker
Mr. Thomas A. Russo is the Managing Member of Gardner Russo & Gardner LLC, where he oversees $10 billion of “global value” equity investments invested through Semper Vic Partnerships as well as separately managed accounts. Mr. Russo is a Graduate of Dartmouth College (BA, 1977), and a Graduate of Stanford Business and Law Schools (MBA/JD, 1984). Memberships include Dean’s Advisory Council for Stanford Law School, Dartmouth College’s President’s Leadership Council, Heilbrunn Center for Graham & Dodd Investing (Columbia), Facing History and Ourselves, Winston Churchill Foundation of the United States, Storm King Art Center.
summary: The speaker argues that the best investment targets are traditional businesses with a unique 'capacity to suffer' while growing intrinsic value, citing Berkshire Hathaway as the prime example. This resilience is demonstrated through long-term capital preservation strategies, such as holding massive cash reserves to avoid inflation and credit risks, rather than chasing short-term yields. The thesis extends to specific holdings like Amazon, Google, and MasterCard, which are valued for their ability to endure challenges, invest aggressively in growth or digital conversion, and maintain strong competitive positions over the long term.

claims.claim: Amazon is noted for having a strong capacity to suffer, though the speaker is unsure if it will ever report a profit.
claims.quote: Amazon. Amazon's way out, even beyond you guys. I'm not sure that they'll ever report a profit. But they certainly have the capacity to suffer. So do their shareholders. Well, of course they get rewarded for it.
claims.speaker: Thomas Russo

claims.claim: Berkshire Hathaway is described as the best example of a traditional business with the capacity to suffer and grow intrinsic value.
claims.quote: Berkshire is the best one. That's why I learned this subject. Warren talks about it all the time. But Geico's a great example. Much like confectionery in China, it's expensive, it turns out, to bring on an auto insured.
claims.speaker: Thomas Russo

claims.claim: Berkshire Hathaway took $5 billion to invest for 18 years to insure a portfolio against decline, demonstrating a unique culture and capital balance sheet.
claims.quote: In return, we received $5.3 billion to invest, unfettered, for 18 years. It was non-callable and it had no collateral posting requirements, which are the killers in this business.
claims.speaker: Thomas Russo

claims.claim: Warren Buffett kept $50 billion in cash earning 0.01% rather than investing in bonds yielding 4%, suffering a $2 billion annual difference to avoid inflation and credit risks.
claims.quote: The difference between 4% and 0.1% on $50 billion is $2 billion a year. That's the amount he suffered by under reporting, because he kept his money in liquid treasuries.
claims.speaker: Thomas Russo

claims.claim: Google incubates projects that burden profit with ideas of where they might end up, even if they don't always succeed, showing extraordinary power.
claims.quote: You know, you think about all the kind of projects that Google incubates, burdening profit with an idea, maybe, of where it'll end up, but in some cases not even. That's extraordinarily powerful.
claims.speaker: Thomas Russo

claims.claim: The speaker highlights Brown-Forman's family control as a virtue that allows for long-term focus and integrity, noting the company successfully grew internationally despite initial unprofitability.
claims.quote: And Brown-Forman's the last one I'll talk about. It's ironic. This is how screwed up America is. In Brown-Forman's case, what I call the virtue of family control, which is the alignment of interest for the long term
claims.speaker: Thomas Russo

claims.claim: The speaker views MasterCard as a great holding aligned with global commerce growth, noting its capacity to suffer through investment and its strong position in developing markets.
claims.quote: It's a great question. It's a big holding. It's really aligned to capture exactly the same forces that I'm looking at in the consumer portfolio, which is the rise of commerce globally. And understand that, at the moment, 85% of the global commerce is still cash. And MasterCard set about to convert that.
claims.speaker: Thomas Russo

claims.claim: The speaker believes MasterCard has significant work ahead in converting cash to digital commerce, making it a worthy hold even if less undervalued than before.
claims.quote: So it's expensive. It's gone up from $20 a share to $90 since I bought it in 2010. So at $90 it's not as compellingly undervalued, but I still think they have so much work ahead of them that it's a worthy hold.
claims.speaker: Thomas Russo

claims.claim: The speaker praises CEO Ajay Banga for reinvesting operating income into growth projects and changing the company's orientation to focus on long-term strength.
claims.quote: He also had a capacity to understand that his job was to deliver to his successor a much stronger company. That's his view. And so every year since he's been at the helm, the gross dollar volume of business, pass-through of their business, is growing about 13% a year.
claims.speaker: Thomas Russo

claims.claim: The speaker values MasterCard's lower margins as evidence of its aggressive investment strategy and competitive position compared to Visa.
claims.quote: And I like that, I think, competitive position that you see with that lower margin, because they're investing more. AUDIENCE: Thank you. Wonderful presentation. THOMAS RUSSO: Thank you.
claims.speaker: Thomas Russo
